These, monks, are ten things that are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and difficult to obtain in the world.

3. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten obstacles:

4. Laziness and lack of initiative are obstacles to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are obstacles to one's appearance. Engaging in things that are not suitable are obstacles to health. Bad friendship is an obstacle to morality. Lack of restraint of the senses is an obstacle to the holy life. Deceiving friends is an obstacle to friendship. Not reciting or studying is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to hear and lack of questioning are obstacles to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are obstacles to the <term>dhamma</term> <gloss>teachings/principles</gloss>. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten obstacles to those ten things that are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and difficult to obtain in the world.

5. Regarding these ten things, monks, which are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten sustaining conditions:

6. Diligence and initiative are the sustenance for wealth. Grooming and adornment are the sustenance for one's appearance. Engaging in suitable things is the sustenance for health. Good friendship is the sustenance for morality. Restraint of the senses is the sustenance for the holy life. Not deceiving friends is the sustenance for friendship. Recitation and study are the sustenance for great learning. The desire to hear and questioning are the sustenance for wisdom. Application and reflection are the sustenance for the <term>dhamma</term> <gloss>teachings/principles</gloss>. Right practice is the sustenance for the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten sustaining conditions for those ten things that are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and difficult to obtain in the world.

[context] What ten?
[context] It’s when someone kills living creatures. They’re violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to all living beings.
They steal. With the intention to commit theft, they take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.
They commit sexual misconduct. They have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.
They lie. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
They backbite. They repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. And so they divide those who are harmonious, supporting division, delighting in division, loving division, speaking words that promote division.
They speak harshly. They use the kinds of words that are cruel, nasty, hurtful, offensive, bordering on anger, not leading to immersion.
They talk nonsense. Their speech is untimely, and is neither factual nor beneficial. It has nothing to do with the teaching or the training. Their words have no value, and are untimely, unreasonable, rambling, and pointless.
They’re covetous. They covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’
They have ill will and malicious intentions: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, slain, destroyed, or annihilated!’
They have wrong view. Their perspective is distorted:
‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’
Someone with these ten qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.
Someone with ten qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.
What ten?
It’s when someone gives up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.
They give up stealing. They don’t, with the intention to commit theft, take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.
They give up sexual misconduct. They don’t have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They don’t have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.
They give up lying. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.
They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.
They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.
They’re content. They don’t covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’
They have a kind heart and loving intentions: ‘May these sentient beings live free of enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy!’
They have right view, an undistorted perspective:
‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. [context] Someone with these ten qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.”

MAHĀ-VAGGA. [III. 61. 2.]

I say to them: If that is so, then venerable ones, you will be killers of living beings because of prior deeds, you will be takers of what is not given because of prior deeds, you will be unchaste because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of falsehood because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of malicious words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of harsh words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of frivolous gossip because of prior deeds, you will be covetous because of prior deeds, you will be malevolent because of prior deeds, and you will hold wrong views because of prior deeds. But for those who fall back on prior deeds as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort, nor the thought that this is to be done or this is not to be done. Because the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done cannot be truly and reliably found, those who dwell with confused mindfulness and lack of self-guarding do not have a firm foundation for a doctrine of righteous living.

This, monks, is my first refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

3. Regarding this, monks, to those ascetics and brahmins who hold the view and opinion that whatever a person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling—is all due to the creation of a supreme deity <term>issaranimmânahetu</term> <gloss>due to the creation of a god</gloss>, I approach them and say: Is it true, venerable ones, that you hold this view and opinion?

If, when asked, they answer yes.

I say to them: If that is so, then venerable ones, you will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a god . . . [and so on] . . . you will be holders of wrong views because of the creation of a god. But for those who fall back on the creation of a god as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort, nor the thought that this is to be done or this is not to be done. Because the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done cannot be truly and reliably found, those who dwell with confused mindfulness and lack of self-guarding do not have a firm foundation for a doctrine of righteous living.

This, monks, is my second refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

# The Great Section <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

To them, I say this: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be those who take life <note>original: pânâtipâtino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who take what is not given <note>original: adinnâdâyino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who are unchaste <note>original: abrahmacârino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak lies <note>original: musâvâdino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak malicious words <note>original: pisuṇâvâcâ</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak harsh words <note>original: pharusâvâcâ</note> because of past actions; you would be those who engage in idle chatter <note>original: samphappalâpino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who are covetous <note>original: abhijhâluno</note> because of past actions; you would be those who have ill-will in their hearts <note>original: vyâpannacittâ</note> because of past actions; and you would be those who hold wrong views <note>original: micchâdiṭṭhikâ</note> because of past actions."

Monks, for those who fall back on past actions as the essential truth <note>original: sârato paccâgacchatam</note>, there is neither desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: "This should be done," or "This should not be done." Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics <note>original: samaṇavâdo</note>.

Monks, this is my first righteous refutation <note>original: sahadhammiko niggaho</note> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions.

3. Regarding this, monks, there are those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions as this: "Whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <note>original: issaranimmânahetu</note>." I approach them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a view and such an opinion: that whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

If, when asked this by me, they admit it is so.

Then I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be those who take life because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... <note>The text indicates a repetition of the previous list of ten unwholesome actions</note> ...you would be those who hold wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is neither desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: 'This should be done,' or 'This should not be done.' Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics."

Monks, this is my second righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions.

# THE CLOUD CHAPTER <note>original: Valāhakavagga</note>

102.

1. Monks <note>original: bhikkhave</note>, there are these four types of clouds. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain <note>original: gajjitā no vassitā</note>... <note>the text elides the intermediate types here</note> ...and the one that both thunders and rains.
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. In the same way, monks, these four people who resemble clouds are found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain... and the one who both thunders and rains.

3. And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching <note>original: dhammam</note>, namely: the discourses <note>original: suttam</note>, the mixed prose and verse <note>original: geyyam</note>, the explanations <note>original: veyyākaraṇam</note>, the verses <note>original: gātham</note>, the inspired utterances <note>original: udānam</note>, the "as it was said" quotations <note>original: itivuttakam</note>, the birth stories <note>original: jātakam</note>, the marvelous qualities <note>original: abbhutadhammam</note>, and the interpretations <note>original: vedallam</note>. Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" <note>original: dukkhan</note>... <note>the text elides the second and third truths</note> ...he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" <note>original: dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā</note>.
Thus, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain. I say this person is like that cloud which thunders but does not rain.

4. And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

5. And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who neither thunders nor rains. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

6. And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, I say this person is like that.

5. Furthermore, monks, when a monk reflects on form <note>original: "rūpa"</note>, his mind does not leap forward, does not grow clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated regarding form. But when he reflects on the formless <note>original: "arūpa"</note>, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the formless. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from forms. Those <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss> and the distress and burning heat that arise based on form, he is freed from them, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from forms.

6. Furthermore, monks, when a monk reflects on personality <note>original: "sakkāya"</note>, his mind does not leap forward, does not grow clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated regarding personality. But when he reflects on the cessation of personality, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the cessation of personality. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from personality. Those <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss> and the distress and burning heat that arise based on personality, he is freed from them, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from personality.

The delight in sensual pleasure does not lie latent in him; the delight in ill-will does not lie latent in him; the delight in harming does not lie latent in him; the delight in form does not lie latent in him; the delight in personality does not lie latent in him. Because the delight in sensual pleasure is not latent in him, and the delight in ill-will, harming, form, and personality are not latent in him, this monk, monks, is called one without latent tendencies. He has cut off <term>taṇhā</term> <gloss>craving</gloss>, untwisted the <term>samyojana</term> <gloss>fetters</gloss>, and by the correct realization of pride, he has made an end of suffering.

These, monks, are the five elements of escape.

However, when he reflects on the formless <note>original: "arūpa"</note>, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the formless. That mind of his is well-developed, well-cultivated, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from forms. And the <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss> <note>original: "ye ca rūpapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātapariḷāhā"</note>, the vexations and burning fevers that arise based on form, from those he is liberated, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from forms.

6. Furthermore, monks, when a monk reflects on the personality <note>original: "sakkāya"</note>, his mind does not leap forward, does not grow clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated regarding the personality. However, when he reflects on the cessation of personality <note>original: "sakkāyanirodha"</note>, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the cessation of personality. That mind of his is well-developed, well-cultivated, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from the personality. And the <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss>, the vexations and burning fevers that arise based on the personality, from those he is liberated, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from the personality.

For him, the delight in sense-desire does not lie dormant, the delight in ill-will does not lie dormant, the delight in harming does not lie dormant, the delight in form does not lie dormant, and the delight in personality does not lie dormant. Because the delight in sense-desire does not lie dormant for him, nor the delight in ill-will, nor the delight in harming, nor the delight in form, nor the delight in personality, this monk, monks, is called one who has no latent tendencies. He has cut off craving <note>original: "taṇha"</note>, he has unrolled the fetter <note>original: "samyojana"</note>, and through the complete penetration of conceit, he has made an end to suffering <note>original: "dukkhassa"</note>.

These, monks, are the five elements of escape.

[context] The Longer Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation
[context] So I have heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.
What four?
It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
1. Observing the Body
1.1. Mindfulness of Breathing
And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the body?
It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.
Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.
Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’
Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’
They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’
They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’
It’s like a deft lathe-turner or lathe-turner’s apprentice. When drawing a long pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a long pull,’ and when drawing a short pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a short pull.’
And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.
Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.
That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.
1.2. The Postures
Furthermore, when a mendicant is walking they know: ‘I am walking.’ When standing they know: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting they know: ‘I am sitting.’ And when lying down they know: ‘I am lying down.’
Whatever posture their body is in, they know it.
And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
[context] They meditate observing, with respect to the body, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.
[context] Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.
[context] That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, in a market town of the Kuru people named Kammāsadhamma. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks!" and they replied, "Venerable Sir!" The Blessed One said this: "This is the direct path, monks, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of suffering and distress, for the attainment of the noble path, and for the realization of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>extinguishment/liberation</gloss>, which is the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, crosses his legs, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness in front of him. Always mindful, he breathes in, and mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands, "I am breathing in long." Breathing out long, he understands, "I am breathing out long." Breathing in short, he understands, "I am breathing in short." Breathing out short, he understands, "I am breathing out short." He trains, "I shall breathe in, experiencing the whole body." He trains, "I shall breathe out, experiencing the whole body." He trains, "I shall breathe in, calming the bodily formation." He trains, "I shall breathe out, calming the bodily formation."

What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mental qualities in mental qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty places, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.

Breathing in long, he knows, 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, he knows, 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, he knows, 'I breathe out short.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.'"

68. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ භික්ඛු සුඛස්ස ච පහානා දුක්ඛස්ස ච පහානා පුබ්බෙව සොමනස්සදොමනස්සානං අත්ථඞ්ගමා අදුක්ඛමසුඛං උපෙක්ඛාසතිපාරිසුද්ධිං චතුත්ථං ඣානං උපසම්පජ්ජ විහරති. සො ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

සෙය්‍යථාපි මහාරාජ පුරිසො ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන සබ්බං පාරුපිතවා නිසින්නො අස්ස, නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන අප්ඵුටං අස්ස, එවමෙව ඛො මහාරාජ භික්ඛු ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

ඉදම්පි ඛො මහාරාජ සන්දිට්ඨිකං සාමඤ්ඤඵලං පුරිමෙහි සන්දිට්ඨිකෙහි සාමඤ්ඤඵලෙහි අභික්කන්තතරඤ්ච පණීතතරඤ්ච.

69. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ සො භික්ඛු එවං සමාහිතෙ චිත්තෙ පරිසුද්ධෙ පරියොදාතෙ අනඞ්ගණෙ විගතූපක්කිලෙසෙ මුදුභූතෙ කම්මනීයෙ ඨිතෙ ආනෙඞ්ජප්පත්තාය චිත්තං අභිනය්‍යති අභිහරිති. සො එවං පජානාති: “අයං ඛො මෙ කායො රූපී චාතුම්මහාභූතිකො මාතාපෙත්තිකසම්භවො ඔදනකුම්මාසුපචයො අනිච්චුච්ඡාදනපරිමද්දන-භෙදනවිද්ධංසනධම්මො. ඉදඤ්ච පන මෙ විඤ්ඤාණං එත්ථ සිතං එත්ථ පටිබද්ධ”න්ති.

70. සෙය්‍යථාපි මහාරාජ මණි වෙළුරියො සුභො ජාතිමා අට්ඨංසො සුපරිකම්මකතො අච්ඡො විප්පසන්නො අනාවිලො සබ්බාකාරසම්පන්නො, තත්ථායං සුත්තං ආවුතං නීලං වා පೀತං වා ලොහිතං වා ඔදාතං වා පණ්ඩුසුත්තං වා. තමෙනං චක්ඛුමා පුරිසො හත්ථෙ කරිත්වා පච්චවෙක්ඛෙය්‍ය “අයං ඛො මණි වෙළුරියො සුභො ජාතිමා අට්ඨංසො සුපරිකම්මකතො, අච්ඡො විප්පසන්නො අනාවිලො සබ්බාකාරසම්පන්නො. තත්ථායං සුත්තං ආවුතං නීලං වා පೀತං වා ලොහිතං වා ඔදාතං වා පණ්ඩුසුත්තං වා”ති.

[context] Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
[context] They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.
[context] It’s like when a deft bathroom attendant or their apprentice pours bath powder into a bronze dish, sprinkling it little by little with water. They knead it until the ball of bath powder is soaked and saturated with moisture, spread through inside and out; yet no moisture oozes out.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.
This, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.6. Second Absorption
Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time.
But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.7. Third Absorption
Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water. There’s no part of them that’s not soaked with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.8. Fourth Absorption
Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.
In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3. The Eight Knowledges
4.3.3.1. Knowledge and Vision
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
They understand:
‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.
And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’
Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.
And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it:
‘This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.2. Mind-Made Body
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
Suppose a person was to draw a reed out from its sheath.
They’d think:
‘This is the reed, this is the sheath. The reed and the sheath are different things. The reed has been drawn out from the sheath.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a sword out from its scabbard.
They’d think:
‘This is the sword, this is the scabbard. The sword and the scabbard are different things. The sword has been drawn out from the scabbard.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a snake out from its slough.
They’d think:
‘This is the snake, this is the slough. The snake and the slough are different things. The snake has been drawn out from the slough.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.3. Psychic Powers
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.
Suppose a deft potter or their apprentice had some well-prepared clay. They could produce any kind of pot that they like.
Or suppose a deft ivory-carver or their apprentice had some well-prepared ivory. They could produce any kind of ivory item that they like.
Or suppose a deft goldsmith or their apprentice had some well-prepared gold. They could produce any kind of gold item that they like.
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.4. Clairaudience
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.
With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
Suppose there was a person traveling along the road. They’d hear the sound of drums, clay drums, horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms. They’d think: ‘That’s the sound of drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of clay drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.
[context] With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
[context] This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.

In this same way, great king, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with this pleasure born of seclusion <note>referring to the rapture and ease previously described in the meditation stages</note>. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this pleasure born of seclusion.

This, too, great king, is a visible fruit of asceticism, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of asceticism.

68. Furthermore, great king, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth jhāna <note>a state of meditative absorption</note>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity. He sits having suffused this body with a mind that is pure and bright. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by a mind that is pure and bright.

Just as if, great king, a man were sitting having covered his entire body with a white cloth, and there were no part of his entire body that was not covered by the white cloth, in this same way, great king, a monk sits having suffused this body with a mind that is pure and bright. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by a mind that is pure and bright.

This, too, great king, is a visible fruit of asceticism, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of asceticism.

69. Furthermore, great king, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision. He understands thus: "This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished on rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being worn away and abraded, to breaking and destruction. And this consciousness of mine is bound to it and dependent on it."

70. Just as if, great king, there were a beryl gem, beautiful, of eight facets, well-cut, clear, transparent, unclouded, and perfect in all its qualities, and through it were threaded a string of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden color. A man with good vision, taking it in his hand, would reflect upon it thus: "This is a beryl gem, beautiful, of eight facets, well-cut, clear, transparent, unclouded, and perfect in all its qualities. And through it is threaded a string of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden color."

In the same way, Great King, a monk drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with a happiness <note>referring to the third meditative state</note> that is free from rapture. There is no part of his entire body untouched by this happiness that is free from rapture.

This, Great King, is a fruit of reclusive life <note>term: sāmaññaphala</note> <gloss>the result of living as a monk</gloss> visible in this very life, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of reclusive life.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the giving up of pleasure and the giving up of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body untouched by that pure, bright mind.

Just as if, Great King, a man were to sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by the white cloth; in the same way, Great King, a monk sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body untouched by that pure, bright mind.

This, Great King, is a fruit of reclusive life visible in this very life, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of reclusive life.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when the mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision. He understands thus: "This body of mine has form, it is composed of the four great elements, born of a mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being worn away, broken up, and dissolved. And this consciousness <note>term: viññāṇa</note> of mine is supported here and bound up here."

70. Just as if, Great King, there were a beautiful beryl gem <note>term: veḷuriya</note> <gloss>lapis lazuli or similar precious stone</gloss> of the purest water, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. And through it was strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown. A man with good sight, taking it in his hand, would reflect: "This is a beautiful beryl gem of the purest water, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. Through it is strung this thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown."

In this same way, Great King, the monk saturates, drenches, fills, and suffuses this very body with this pleasure born of seclusion <note>referring to the rapture and physical ease attained in the preceding meditative states</note>. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pleasure born of seclusion.

This, too, Great King, is a visible fruit of recluseship, more excellent and sublime than the previous visible fruits of recluseship.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and sorrow, the monk enters and remains in the fourth jhāna <note>meditative absorption</note>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity. He sits having suffused this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pure, bright mind.

Just as if, Great King, a man were sitting having covered himself from head to foot with a white cloth, such that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by the white cloth, in the same way, Great King, the monk sits having suffused this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pure, bright mind.

This, too, Great King, is a visible fruit of recluseship, more excellent and sublime than the previous visible fruits of recluseship.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when his mind is thus composed, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of impurities, pliant, workable, established, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision. He understands thus: "This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and pressed, to breaking up and destruction. And this consciousness of mine is bound to it, dependent on it."

70. Just as if, Great King, there were a beryl gem, beautiful, natural, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, limpid, unclouded, and perfect in all its qualities, through which a thread was strung—blue, yellow, red, white, or brown. A person with eyes, taking it in their hand, would reflect upon it: "This is a beryl gem, beautiful, natural, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, limpid, unclouded, and perfect in all its qualities. And through it is strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or brown."

<summary>This passage describes the attainment of the fourth meditative absorption and the subsequent development of insight into the material nature of the body and its relationship with consciousness.</summary>

17. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘මාතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පිතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භාතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භගිනී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පුත්තො මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ධීතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘පජාපතී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘ඤාතකා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘මිත්තා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති,-- ‘ගාමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘නිගමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ඛෙත්තං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘වත්ථු මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘හිරඤ්ඤං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘සුවණ්ණං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘සිප්පං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි සික්ඛාවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

18. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘දුක්කර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති -- ‘කසුකර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ‘දුබ්බර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න සුවර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න උස්සාහමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න විස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘න රමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘න අභිරමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි බො භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

19. කථඤ්ච භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා? ඉධ භික්ඛවෙ භික්ඛු උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො -පෙ- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘බුද්ධං පවචක්ඛාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා.

Pārājikapāḷi—The First Defeat

17. Or, if a <term>sāmaṇeru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss>, being restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "I have a mother, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a father, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a brother, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a sister, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a son, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a daughter, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a wife, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have relatives, they will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have friends, they will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a village, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have a town, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have fields, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have property, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have silver, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have gold, I will live from that," and causes distraction; [ellipses] or, "I have a craft, I will live from that," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is cast aside.

18. Or, if a <term>sāmaṇeru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss>, being restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "It is difficult," and causes distraction; or, "It is tiresome," and causes distraction; "It is unbearable," and causes distraction; or, "It is not easy," and causes distraction; or, "I am unable," and causes distraction; or, "I do not wish to," and causes distraction; or, "I do not find joy," and causes distraction; [ellipses] or, "I do not find pleasure," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is cast aside.

19. And how, monks, is there an expression of weakness and the training is officially renounced? Here, monks, a monk <note>referring to the novice context</note> who is restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "I renounce the Buddha," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is officially renounced.

<summary>This page details specific verbal expressions of restlessness and dissatisfaction made by a novice monk that lead to the abandonment of monastic training.
